text: Viktor Mikhaylovich Vasnetsov (Russian: Ви́ктор Миха́йлович Васнецо́в; 15 May [O.S. 3 May] 1848 – 23 July 1926) was a Russian painter and draughtsman known for his work in mythological and historical subjects. He is regarded as a co-founder of Russian folklorist and romantic nationalistic painting and a key figure in the Russian Revivalist movement. Born in 1848 in the village of Lopyal in the Vyatka Governorate, he was the second of seven children, with only one sister surviving past four months after birth. His father, Mikhail Vasilievich Vasnetsov (1823–1870), was a member of the priesthood, a scholar of natural sciences and astronomy, and philosophically inclined; his grandfather was an icon painter. Two of Mikhail’s six sons, Viktor and Apollinary, became notable painters, while three became schoolteachers and one a Russian folklorist. In Lopyal, Viktor began painting landscapes and scenes of village life, recalling his childhood in a letter to Vladimir Stasov, stating he "had lived with peasant children and liked them not as a narodnik but as a friend." From age ten, he studied at a seminary in Vyatka, spending summers in the merchant village of Ryabovo, where he worked for a local icon shopkeeper and assisted exiled Polish artist Michał Elwiro Andriolli in executing frescoes for Vyatka's Alexander Nevsky Cathedral. After graduating, he moved to Saint Petersburg to study art, raising funds by auctioning his paintings *Woman Harvester* and *Milk-maid* (both 1867). He initially failed to enter the Imperial Academy of Arts in August 1867 but succeeded in August 1868. During his time at the Academy, he befriended Ivan Kramskoi, whom he referred to as his teacher, and became close to fellow student Ilya Repin. Though he initially avoided mythological and historical subjects, he received a small silver medal for his composition *Christ and Pontius Pilate Before the People*. In the early 1870s, he produced numerous engravings, including *Provincial Bookseller* (1870) and *A Boy with a Bottle of Vodka* (1872), both of which won bronze medals at the 1874 World Fair in London. He also began creating genre paintings such as *Peasant Singers* (1873) and *Moving House* (1876), which were well received by democratic circles. In 1876, Repin invited him to join the Peredvizhniki colony in Paris, where he studied classical and contemporary art, including academist and Impressionist works. While in France, he painted *Acrobats* (1877), produced prints, and exhibited at the Salon. It was in Paris that he became fascinated with fairy-tale subjects, beginning work on *Ivan Tsarevich Riding a Grey Wolf* and *The Firebird*. He was a model for Sadko in Repin’s painting *Sadko*. In 1877, he returned to Moscow. In the late 1870s, he focused on illustrating Russian fairy tales and the epic poem Bylinas, producing major works such as *The Knight at the Crossroads* (1878), *Prince Igor's Battlefield* (1878), *Three Princesses of the Underground Kingdom* (completed 1884), *The Flying Carpet* (1880), and *Alionushka* (1881). These works were initially dismissed by critics, including prominent connoisseur Pavel Mikhailovich Tretyakov, who refused to buy them, though their popularity grew in the 1880s after he turned to religious subjects and created a series of icons for Savva Mamontov’s Abramtsevo estate. From 1884 to 1889, he was commissioned to paint frescoes in St Vladimir's Cathedral in Kiev, a project criticized by art critic Vladimir Stasov as sacrilegious and by Dmitry Filosofov as "the first bridge over 200 years-old gulf separating different classes of Russian society." While in Kiev, he befriended Mikhail Vrubel, who was also involved in the cathedral’s decoration, and during this time taught the younger artist. In Kiev, he completed *Ivan Tsarevich Riding a Grey Wolf* and began his most famous painting, *The Bogatyrs*. In 1885, he traveled to Italy and worked on stage designs and costumes for Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera *The Snow Maiden*. In the following decades, he expanded into other media. In 1897, he collaborated with his brother Apollinary on the theatrical design of Rimsky-Korsakov’s premiere *Sadko*. At the turn of the century, he developed his signature "fairy-tale" style of Russian Revivalist architecture, with his first acclaimed design being a church at Abramtsevo (1882) in collaboration with Vasily Polenov. In 1894, he designed his own mansion in Moscow, and in 1898, he designed the Russian pavilion at the World Fair in Paris. In 1904, he designed the façade of the Tretyakov Gallery, his most renowned "fairy-tale" building. Between 1906 and 1911, he designed mosaics for Alexander Nevsky Cathedral in Warsaw and was involved in the design of Alexander Nevsky Cathedral in Moscow. In 1912, he was granted a noble title by Czar Nicholas II. In 1914, he designed a revenue stamp for voluntary collection for victims of World War I. Before the Russian Revolution, he became a regent of the Tretyakov Gallery and allocated a significant portion of his income to the State Historical Museum, enabling the acquisition of a large part of its collection. After the October Revolution, he advocated for the removal of some religious paintings from churches to the Tretyakov Gallery. In 1915, he participated in designing a military uniform for the Russian army’s Victory parade in Berlin and Constantinople and is credited with creating the *budenovka* (initially named *bogatyrka*), a military hat modeled after the cone-shaped helmets of Kievan Rus’. Vasnetsov died in Moscow in 1926 at the age of 78. A minor planet, 3586 Vasnetsov, discovered in 1978 by Lyudmila Zhuravlyova, is named after Viktor and Apollinary Vasnetsov. In the film *Elizabeth: The Golden Age*, Vasnetsov’s painting of Ivan the Terrible is anachronistically shown as existing during Ivan’s lifetime and being sent to England when he offers to marry Queen Elizabeth I. His grandson, Andrei Vladimirovich Vasnetsov (1924–2009), was named People's Artist of the USSR.
